delta_name: Wire delay mechanism shifts from RC-dominated to coupling-capacitance-dominated
at_28nm: Wire delay was modeled as Elmore delay dominated by self-capacitance (Cwire = εA/d). Engineers focused on total wire length and avoided long parallel runs but did not routinely model coupling as a separate entity. RC extraction used a single total capacitance number. Timing budgets allocated wire delay as a fraction of total path delay without detailed coupling attribution.
at_7nm_5nm: Coupling capacitance represents 40-60% of total wire capacitance at 7nm. The same physical wire carries 2-3x more delay if an aggressor net runs adjacent and switches simultaneously. Delta delay from crosstalk can add 10-30ps to a data path. STA tools must now compute two delay values (victim quiet, victim switching) per net, not one. Engineers analyze aggressor-victim pairs for every critical net.
why_it_changed: Metal pitch compresses at 7nm: line width shrinks to ~20-30nm while spacing shrinks to ~20-30nm. Capacitance to adjacent metal (Ccoupling = ε/d) grows while capacitance to substrate (Cself = εA/d) shrinks. The ratio Ccoupling/Cself inverts from roughly 0.3 at 28nm to roughly 1.5-2.0 at 7nm. EUV lithography partially recovers line roughness but does not restore the coupling ratio.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer routes critical paths using minimum-spacing rules without checking coupling, assuming timing margin will absorb the difference. At 7nm the delta delay from coupling on a 200ps path is 15-30ps — larger than the margin. The symptom is timing that passes signoff STA but fails silicon at SS corner because coupling was not modeled with worst-case aggressor switching.
workflow_impact: Timing-driven routing (TDR) tools absorbed coupling-aware routing as a mandatory mode, not a toggle. The TDR stage now runs full noise analysis internally and must route critical nets with shielding or increased spacing. This adds 2-4 hours to each routing iteration.

delta_name: Clock distribution from H-trees to mesh/trunk hybrid
at_28nm: H-tree clock distribution with standard library buffers was the default topology. Clock insertion delay was 200-500ps; skew of 20-30ps was achievable with careful buffer placement. Clock planning was done post-placement. Designers trusted that CTS tool optimization would solve skew problems.
at_7nm_5nm: H-trees are insufficient for >500MHz designs at 7nm. Clock wire lengths exceed 3-5mm causing >100ps of wire delay that buffers alone cannot equalize. Mesh topologies (grid of trunks with leaf distribution) are used for the top-level clock, supplemented by local CTS. Mesh planning must begin at floorplan stage, not post-placement. Double-patterning constraints on clock metals require shielding or coloring-aware routing.
why_it_changed: Clock wire resistance per unit length increases as wire width shrinks (R = ρL/A). At 7nm, the resistivity of copper does not change but the cross-sectional area of a clock trunk is 4-6x smaller than at 28nm. A 5mm clock wire that was 10Ω at 28nm becomes 50-60Ω at 7nm — the buffer driving it cannot equalize delay across the tree fast enough. The physics forces a shorter-hop mesh topology.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer designs the clock tree after placement, trusting CTS to handle skew. At 7nm, post-placement clock planning produces >50ps skew and >200ps insertion delay because the floorplan does not support an H-tree geometry. The symptom is clock skew that cannot be closed even after 10 CTS iterations — the floorplan is wrong for an H-tree topology.
workflow_impact: Clock planning moved from a CTS tool output to a floorplan-stage input. Physical architects now draw clock trunk/mesh geometry before placement starts, and placement tools are constrained to honor it. This added a new floorplan review gate (clock feasibility check) that did not exist at 28nm.

delta_name: Multi-patterning decomposes placement from a continuous to a constrained-discrete problem
at_28nm: Metal layers used single-pass lithography. Routing rules were spacing and width minimums; coloring was not a constraint. Placement was continuous: cells could be placed at any legal location without lithographic cross-talk concerns. Routing tools respected spacing but not color assignment.
at_7nm_5nm: M1-M4 require multi-patterning (SAIL, SADP, or LELE) for sub-resolution features. Every routing segment on affected layers must be assigned to one of two or four color groups that are physically separated on the wafer. Violations of color assignment (coloring conflicts) are DRC violations equivalent to spacing violations. Placement must avoid creating coloring conflicts by design — spacing rules change depending on which color a neighboring segment belongs to.
why_it_changed: At 28nm, 193nm immersion lithography could print ~80nm features. At 7nm, EUV or DUV multi-patterning is required; the smallest features are resolved by decomposing a single drawn layer into 2-4 mask exposures. The decomposition must be consistent with design rules: same-color features must not violate spacing, and the decomposition must be unambiguous. Design tools must track color assignment to ensure the layout decomposes cleanly.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer uses standard spacing rules without considering color. When routing a bus through a channel, adjacent wires that are placed at minimum spacing are assumed legal. At 7nm, two adjacent minimum-pitch wires of the same color on a double-patterned layer violate DRC because they must be on different masks and there is no physical space for two masks between them. The symptom is a sudden explosion of coloring DRC violations after detailed routing, requiring rerouting of entire bus structures.
workflow_impact: Routing tools absorbed coloring-aware routing as a hard constraint mode. Placement tools added coloring conflict prediction and cell padding for multi-patterned layers. This added 1-3 hours to placement runs and 2-4 hours to routing iterations at 7nm.

delta_name: IR/EM from late-stage signoff check to floorplan-stage design constraint
at_28nm: Power grid was designed after placement, using pre-characterized cell power models and a standard grid template. IR drop was verified as a signoff check with >10% margin considered safe. EM was a reliability checkbox for wide power straps only; current density limits were conservative and rarely binding. Engineers rarely revisited the power grid after initial placement.
at_7nm_5nm: Power grid design must begin before placement. Metal widths that were safe at 28nm (10µm power straps) are too wide at 7nm (EM is still okay but routing resources are consumed). Metal widths that save resources (2µm straps) may violate EM at operating current. The power grid must be co-designed with the floorplan: strap locations, widths, and via counts must be set before cell placement, and IR drop must be budgeted as a timing variable, not a reliability margin.
why_it_changed: Wire current density (J = I/A) increases as wires shrink. A 1µm-wide power strap carrying 10mA at 28nm is J=10mA/µm. The same current at 7nm on a 0.2µm strap is J=50mA/µm — a 5x increase. EM failure mechanisms (void formation, electromigration) scale with current density. At 7nm, EM limits are reached on straps that look wide by 28nm standards. Additionally, self-heating in narrow copper wires raises local temperature by 20-40°C, further reducing EM lifetime.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer designs the power grid after placement and adds straps or vias as needed to pass IR/EM signoff. At 7nm, the grid geometry is locked in before placement starts. Adding straps post-placement disrupts cell placement; adding vias requires routing access that may not exist. The symptom is an IR drop violation that cannot be fixed without re-floorplanning — a 3-5 day delay.
workflow_impact: Power grid synthesis moved from a place-and-route tool feature to a physical architect deliverable. IR drop analysis must be completed at floorplan stage before placement begins, not as a post-placement signoff check.

delta_name: Utilization targets drop 10-20 percentage points due to routing resource exhaustion
at_28nm: Core utilization of 78-85% was achievable and expected. Routing layers were sufficient to route all signals with standard spacing rules at that density. High utilization was a metric of design efficiency; low utilization implied waste. The constraint was cell area, not routing resources.
at_7nm_5nm: Core utilization of 65-72% is the realistic target for complex designs. Above 70% at 7nm, routing resources are exhausted before all signals can be routed, regardless of cell placement quality. The routing resource constraint (metal tracks) has become the binding constraint, not cell area. The target is lower because routing has more layers but each layer has fewer tracks due to multi-patterning pitch requirements.
why_it_changed: Multi-patterning consumes routing resources without adding capacity. At 28nm, a metal layer provides N tracks. At 7nm with double-patterning, the same drawn layer provides N/2 tracks per mask, requiring both masks to be used to achieve equivalent routing. If color assignment is imperfect (which it often is), effective routing capacity is N*0.7. This means the effective routing track count drops by 30-50% per affected layer even though the process has more metal layers.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer targets 80% utilization and is surprised when placement succeeds but detailed routing produces 50,000+ violations. The symptom is routing congestion that appears after placement, even though the floorplan looks clean in global routing. The fix (lowering utilization) is correct but the engineer waits too long to apply it because their 28nm intuition says 80% is fine.
workflow_impact: Utilization is now set by a floorplan-stage routing resource estimate, not by cell area alone. Placed designs at >72% utilization at 7nm require routing feasibility checks before detailed routing starts. This created a new pre-placement gate (routing resource budgeting) that did not exist at 28nm.

delta_name: Hold closure becomes as hard as setup closure
at_28nm: Hold violations were relatively easy to fix. The standard cell library had sufficient delay range to add hold buffers where needed without significantly affecting setup. Hold margin of 50-100ps was standard. Engineers typically fixed hold violations in the final ECO pass with minimal setup impact. Hold was a known problem with a known solution.
at_7nm_5nm: Hold and setup are in direct conflict. Adding hold buffers (which increases cell delay) consumes routing resources and adds wire length that degrades setup. Clock skew has increased, making hold closure timing-dependent on clock phase relationships, not just data path delay. In designs with multiple clock domains and asynchronous CDC paths, hold violations can cascade across domains. Hold margin has shrunk to 20-30ps.
why_it_changed: Clock skew at 7nm is inherently larger (50-100ps vs 20-30ps at 28nm) due to longer clock wires and less ideal mesh topologies. Hold closure requires data arrival time minus clock arrival time to be positive. Larger clock skew means this margin is smaller. Simultaneously, setup paths are faster (higher frequency) but hold paths are not — the data path delay that helps setup does not help hold because hold is checked against the same clock edge.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer plans to fix hold in the final ECO pass, assuming setup is the hard problem. At 7nm, fixing hold in ECO destroys setup margin because the added hold buffers route through congested areas that add wire delay to critical paths. The symptom is a design that alternates between hold-clean and setup-violation as ECOs are applied — a classic oscillation that extends timing closure by 1-2 weeks.
workflow_impact: Hold fixing moved from a final ECO step to an iterative step throughout the timing closure flow. Engineers now plan hold margins from pre-CTS stage onward. Setup and hold tradeoffs must be tracked jointly, not sequentially.

delta_name: DRC character shifts from spacing/width to via enclosure and pin-access
at_28nm: DRC violations were dominated by spacing and width rules on metal layers. Via rules were simple (enclosure by 3-5µm was standard). Pin access was an optimization concern but not a DRC driver. Minimum-area and density rules existed but were rarely violated by standard flows.
at_7nm_5nm: Via enclosure rules become the dominant DRC category. Vias at 7nm are constrained by cut-array rules (must use 2xN via arrays), via-to-via spacing rules, and minimum/maximum via enclosure that varies by layer. Pin access (the ability of routing to reach a cell's input/output pins) becomes a placement-stage DRC check: if a cell has <85% pin access rate, it cannot be routed legally regardless of spacing rules. Pattern density rules (MCP, CMP) create density windows that must be met per region.
why_it_changed: Via dimensions at 7nm (20-30nm cut size) are small enough that etch variability and overlay error dominate yield. A single via at 7nm has yield <99.9%; a 2x1 or 2x2 via array is required for reliability. This changes the geometry of every connection: a via rule at 7nm is not a single shape but an array of shapes with constraints on array pitch, spacing, and enclosure. Pin access fails because standard cell heights have shrunk (7T vs 9T at 28nm) but pin positions have not scaled proportionally, leaving fewer routing tracks available to reach pins.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer designs cells and placements assuming pin access is a routing-tool problem, not a DRC problem. At 7nm, a cell placed at 90% density has insufficient routing tracks to reach all its pins. The routing tool fails to connect pins and produces open violations that look like LVS mismatches. The fix is cell padding (reducing effective utilization) not routing iteration.
workflow_impact: Placement tools absorbed pin-access DRC as a pre-routing check. Cell padding became a standard placement parameter, not an optimization. This added cell padding optimization to the placement flow and required library characterization to include pin-access models.

delta_name: Signoff timing analysis shifts from OCV to AOCV/POCV and corner explosion
at_28nm: On-chip variation (OCV) was modeled as a flat derating factor applied uniformly across all paths (e.g., ±10% derating). Timing corners were limited: SS/TT/FF at two voltages was sufficient. Path-based analysis was used for critical paths; static timing analysis covered the rest. Library characterization used corner-based models.
at_7nm_5nm: Advanced OCV (AOCV) and statistical OCV (POCV) replace flat derating. Derating factors now vary by path depth (number of logic stages), wire length, and spatial location on the die. Timing corners explode: 7nm designs commonly sign off at 6-10 corners (SS/TT/FF × multiple voltages × temperature × local variation). Libraries are characterized with statistical distribution models, not just corner values.
why_it_changed: At 28nm, within-die variation was small relative to die-to-die variation. A flat derating factor captured most of the variation impact. At 7nm, within-die variation (especially Vt variation from random dopant fluctuation and line-edge roughness) is comparable to die-to-die variation. A path with 20 stages has different statistical variation characteristics than a path with 5 stages. POCV models this by assigning a statistical distribution to each delay element and propagating the distribution through the path, giving a real distribution of path delay rather than a single corner-based value.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer runs timing at SS/TT/FF and declares closure if all paths pass. At 7nm, a design can pass all three corners and still fail statistically — paths with 30+ stages may have a 3-sigma delay 50ps worse than the SS corner estimate due to accumulated local variation. The symptom is timing that passes signoff and fails on silicon, with the failure concentrated in deep combinatorial paths. The fix requires POCV analysis that the engineer did not know to run.
workflow_impact: STA tool runtime increased 3-5x due to statistical analysis and corner explosion. AOCV/POCV characterization added 1-2 weeks to library readiness. Timing signoff now requires a separate statistical timing run in addition to corner-based analysis.

delta_name: Physical verification shifts from custom DRC decks to foundry-mandated signoff decks with pattern-aware rules
at_28nm: Physical verification (DRC/LVS) used custom or vendor-supplied decks that covered spacing, width, and layer rules. Pattern-aware rules were minimal; lithographic simulation was not part of DRC. DFM was a checkbox. Engineers could develop custom DRC decks that were more lenient than foundry rules and still get tapeout approval because wafer acceptance was based on the foundry's own verification.
at_7nm_5nm: Foundries mandate their official signoff decks as the only acceptable verification standard. Pattern-aware rules (checking for lithographic hotspot patterns like jogs, notches, and necking) are integrated into the signoff deck. DFM analysis is required before tapeout: via redundancy, critical area analysis, and metal sliver coverage must be reported. Pattern matching rules catch configurations that are DRC-clean by geometry but lithographically marginal.
why_it_changed: At 28nm, the lithographic process window was wide enough that design geometries within the minimum rule space were reliably printable. At 7nm, the process window is narrow: a jog in a wire that is geometrically legal may have a process window of <5nm of depth of focus. Pattern-aware DRC simulates lithography and flags patterns with insufficient process margin before they cause systematic yield loss.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer runs DRC with a custom or older deck and gets 0 violations. The design is submitted to the foundry and fails their signoff deck, which has additional pattern-aware rules that the custom deck did not check. The delay is 2-4 weeks while the team re-runs DRC with the foundry deck and fixes new violations that were invisible to their previous tool.
workflow_impact: DRC deck management became a project management task, not just a tool task. Teams must maintain the foundry signoff deck version, run DRC with it throughout the flow (not just at the end), and track DFM findings as first-class verification results.

delta_name: Clock skew control shifts from CTS tool optimization to mesh topology planning
at_28nm: Clock skew was primarily a CTS tool problem. The CTS tool analyzed the placed design, computed insertion delay to each leaf, and inserted buffers to equalize delay. Designers set a skew budget (e.g., 30ps) and trusted the tool to meet it. Post-CTS skew of 20-30ps was achievable with iterative optimization. Mesh or structured clock distribution was rare except for high-performance custom blocks.
at_7nm_5nm: Clock skew at 7nm cannot be closed by CTS optimization alone when the floorplan forces long clock wires. Mesh topologies distribute clock power more evenly but shift the skew control problem from the tool to the physical architect. The mesh geometry (trunk width, mesh pitch, leaf buffer placement) must be designed before placement starts. CTS tools work within the mesh topology, not against an arbitrary floorplan. Skew budgets of 10-15ps require mesh planning; 30ps skew budgets are unachievable without it.
why_it_changed: The physics is the same as the clock distribution delta: wire resistance per unit length increases as wire width shrinks. At 28nm, clock wires were wide enough that insertion delay across the die was 200-400ps, manageable by a buffer tree. At 7nm, the same die has clock wire resistance 5-6x higher, making insertion delay variation across the clock network physically larger than a 30ps skew budget. No buffer tree can equalize delay across a high-resistance clock network — the variation must be eliminated by topology (shorter hops via a mesh) not by buffering.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer designs a floorplan without clock planning and expects CTS to handle skew. At 7nm, CTS produces 60-100ps skew because the floorplan geometry forces unequal clock path lengths that no buffer can equalize. The symptom is a skew violation that cannot be fixed by running CTS 10 times — the floorplan must be changed, which is expensive at this stage. Alternatively, the engineer adds more buffers and worsens power consumption by 20-30% trying to close skew in a topology that cannot support it.
workflow_impact: Clock architecture moved from a CTS-stage task to a floorplan-stage task. Physical architects now deliver a clock mesh/trunk specification as a floorplan deliverable. CTS tools are used for leaf-level skew control within a pre-designed mesh, not for end-to-end skew management. This reduced CTS tool runtime (it has less to optimize) but increased floorplan design time.
